body:
Many modern disposables include a USB-C port, so you can recharge them and use the full amount of liquid, which makes a large device much better value. Charging looks simple, and it is, but a few habits make the difference between a battery that lasts and one that fades early or, in rare cases, becomes a problem. This guide explains how to tell whether your device is rechargeable, what you need, how to charge step by step, what the lights mean, how long it takes, what to do and not do while charging, how to protect battery life, what to do when it does not charge and how to dispose of the device at the end. It is written for adults aged 21 and over. Nicotine is addictive.

## Check it is rechargeable
Look for a charging port at the bottom and a Type-C mention on the product page. If there is no port, the device is non-rechargeable, and it cannot be charged. See [rechargeable versus non-rechargeable](/blog/rechargeable-vs-non-rechargeable-disposables/). Do not try to charge a device that has no port, and do not try to force a cable into a port that does not fit.

## What you need
A standard USB-C cable and a USB adapter or computer port. A basic 5V charger is best, and the one that came with your phone is usually fine. Avoid very cheap or unbranded chargers, which may deliver uneven power, and avoid damaged cables. If you use a power bank, make sure it is a reputable one.

## How to charge
1. Plug the cable into the device and the other end into the adapter or port.
2. Check the indicator. Many show red or a pulsing light while charging.
3. Wait about 30 to 60 minutes for a partial charge, or until the light turns green or off, which usually means full.
4. Unplug and use.

Charging a large battery from flat can take longer, up to a couple of hours. The first few minutes may show no light on a very flat battery, so wait before you worry.

## What the lights usually mean
Lights differ between devices, so check the manual, but common patterns include a red or pulsing light while charging, a green or steady light when full and a rapid blink for a fault or a low battery. See [understanding vape device indicator lights](/blog/understanding-vape-device-indicator-lights/).

## While charging
Place it on a hard, flat surface, not on a bed or sofa. Stay nearby and never leave it charging overnight. Keep it away from flammable items and from heat. Keep children and pets away from the device and cable. If the device gets hot, smells or smokes, unplug it and move it away from flammable items.

## Do not use while charging
Unless the manual says pass-through is supported, wait until it is done. Using a device while it charges makes it warmer and puts more strain on the battery. It also risks liquid reaching the port. If you must use it, do so sparingly.

## How long should it last on a charge?
That depends on the battery size and your use. A large-capacity disposable may give hundreds of puffs per charge. Light users may charge once a week, and heavy users every day or two. If a full charge lasts much less than it used to, the battery is wearing. See [mAh, puffs and battery life](/blog/mah-puffs-and-battery-life-how-they-relate/).

## Extend battery life
Charge before the battery is fully empty and avoid heat. See [extending battery life](/blog/how-to-extend-vape-battery-life/). Do not keep a device at a full charge for days. Avoid leaving it in a hot car. Use a quality cable.

## If it does not charge
Try another cable and adapter; see [vape will not charge](/blog/vape-wont-charge-fixes/). Check the port for lint and dirt, and leave a very flat battery connected for 10 to 15 minutes. If there is still no response, the device may be faulty, or the battery may be finished.

## Is it worth charging a disposable?
Yes, for a rechargeable one. The liquid is often the limit, and a battery that has run flat while liquid remains can be revived with a charge. If the device charges and still does not give flavor or vapor, the liquid is probably finished. Do not keep charging a device that does not work.

## A worked example
You have a 30,000-puff rechargeable disposable. After a week of use, the light blinks and vapor is weak. You plug in a USB-C cable and a 5V adapter. The light pulses red. After 45 minutes, it turns green. You unplug and the vapor is back to normal. You repeat this every few days, and you reach the end of the liquid with the battery still working. Without charging, the battery would have run flat long before the liquid.

## Disposal
When the liquid is gone, recycle the device at a hazardous waste or electronics recycling site; see [disposal](/blog/how-to-dispose-of-vapes-and-batteries/). Do not put it in household trash. Do not keep charging a device that no longer works.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Can I use a fast charger?
Usually not needed, and not always suitable. A standard 5V charger is best. If you use a fast charger, check that it supports basic 5V output.

### Can I charge it with a laptop?
Yes, from a standard USB port. Charging may be slower, depending on the port.

### Will charging overnight harm the battery?
It is better not to. Overnight charging means long periods at full charge and unattended heating. Charge during the day, while you are nearby.

### Why does my device stop at 80 percent?
Some devices cut off charging early to protect the battery, or show a light that is not an exact percentage.

### Is it normal for it to take a long time?
A very large battery charged from flat can take a couple of hours. If it takes much longer, try a different cable and adapter.

Browse [disposable vapes](/shop/disposables/). All products are for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## Case studies
### The device that seemed dead
A customer thought a large disposable had finished after two weeks. A charge of 40 minutes restored it, and it lasted another three weeks. Lesson: check whether it is rechargeable before you throw it away.

### The charger that was too fussy
A customer's device would not charge on a fast phone charger, but charged on a basic 5V adapter. Lesson: simple chargers are often the most compatible.

### The overnight habit
A customer charged every night and noticed that the battery faded within two months. Switching to daytime top-ups, with the device on a table, extended it. Lesson: charge when you can watch it, and unplug when full.

## A simple charging routine
Pick a regular time when you are at home, such as the evening, plug the device into a hard surface charger and check it after 45 minutes. Unplug when the light shows it is full. Keep the cable and adapter together so that you do not reach for a poor substitute. A routine means that the battery never goes completely flat, and that you never forget to unplug.

## Reading the light on a typical device
Many devices glow red or pulse while charging and turn green or go dark when full. A fast blink usually signals a fault or a low battery. A steady light while the device is idle may mean it is charging. Always check the maker's guide, because patterns differ.

## What not to charge
Do not charge a device that is hot, wet, swollen or cracked. Do not charge a device that smells odd. Do not charge a non-rechargeable device by forcing a cable into it. If you are unsure, do not charge it, and contact us with your order ID through the [contact page](/contact/).

## Frequently asked questions about charging
### Why does the light blink while charging?
Many devices pulse a light to show that they are charging. A fast blink can signal a fault. Check the manual.

### Can I charge a disposable in a car?
Yes, with a reputable car charger, but do not leave it in a hot car, and do not leave it charging unattended.

### How often should I charge?
When it is low, whenever it is convenient. You do not need to wait for it to run flat.

### Can I charge while using it?
Only if the manual says pass-through is supported. Otherwise wait.

## When you are traveling
If you travel with a rechargeable disposable, pack a short USB-C cable and a small adapter in your carry-on, because devices and batteries must go in carry-on baggage. Charge before you set out, and avoid charging in the airport on public ports you do not trust. Never leave a charging device unattended in a hotel room or a vehicle. See [traveling with vapes](/blog/traveling-with-vapes-airline-rules/) for the rules that apply on flights.

## Keeping a charging spot
Choose one spot at home for charging, such as a hard shelf away from soft furnishings and out of reach of children and pets. Keep the cable and adapter there. A dedicated spot builds a habit, avoids lost cables and keeps devices away from places where they could overheat.
